summary: This informational document updates the conventions for digital signatures on Internet-Drafts defined in RFC 5485. Signatures are made with the Cryptographic Message Syntax and stored as detached files so existing tools are unaffected. This update reflects changes by the RFC Editor in how the process works.

eli5.summary: A teacher signs the corner of a homework page to prove it is real. This updates how the internet's draft documents get such a signature in a separate file.

questions: what changed in rfc 5485 signature conventions
how are internet drafts digitally signed
what content types are used for internet draft signatures
how are text files canonicalized before signing
subtitle: How signatures on Internet-Drafts handle non-ASCII text, new file formats and new content types.

tldr.problem: RFC 5485 defined detached signatures for Internet-Drafts, but text files were expected to be ASCII, and non-ASCII characters were about to appear in drafts.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends the list of signed content types (adding UTF-8 text, HTML and EPUB) and spells out how text and HTML files are canonicalized before signing, while the detached CMS signature stays in a companion .p7s file.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 5485, registers three new object identifiers with IANA, and leaves the security and deployment considerations of RFC 5485 unchanged.

facts.label: Line ending for text and HTML

today: RFC 8358 is an Informational RFC that updates RFC 5485. The metadata for this entry shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why the Signature Rules Needed an Update
sections.content:
RFC 5485 specifies digital signatures on Internet-Drafts. The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) creates a detached signature stored in a separate companion file, so no existing utilities are affected. The IETF Secretariat generates the signature shortly after a draft is posted.

The RFC Editor had just published the first RFC with non-ASCII characters in a text file, following RFC 7997, and the author assumes drafts will soon contain them too. The signature lets anyone check that a draft has not been altered since it was signed. The signing-time shows when the signature was generated and is not meant to be a trusted timestamp.
sections.eli5: The stamp proves a page has not been changed. Because pages may soon use more kinds of letters, the stamping rules need updating.

sections.title: Detached Signature Files
sections.content:
Internet-Draft file names begin with draft- and end with a hyphen, a two-digit version number and a suffix that shows the file type. Going forward, one cannot assume that a .txt file contains only ASCII.

The companion signature file has exactly the same name as the draft with .p7s added to the end, matching the conventions of RFC 5751. For example, draft-ietf-example-widgets-03.txt is signed by draft-ietf-example-widgets-03.txt.p7s.
sections.eli5: Each page gets a sticky note with the same name plus a little tag on the end, so you always know which note belongs to which page.

sections.title: Content Types
sections.content:
The CMS ContentInfo content type MUST always be present and MUST encapsulate the CMS SignedData content type. Because the signature is detached, SignedData MUST NOT encapsulate the Internet-Draft itself.

The eContentType value MUST identify the format of the draft being signed. This RFC expands the list from RFC 5485 to seven formats: ASCII text, UTF-8 text (which includes non-ASCII), HTML, EPUB, XML, PDF and PostScript. Each maps to an object identifier under id-ct, for example id-ct-utf8TextWithCRLF is { id-ct 37 }.
sections.eli5: Each stamp says what kind of paper it is on, such as plain text, web page or PDF, so the checker knows what to expect.

sections.title: Canonicalization
sections.content:
A draft is normally treated as one octet string for signing. Text and HTML files are the exception, because systems end lines differently (a new-line, a carriage-return plus line-feed, or fixed-length padded records), so a single convention is needed for the signature to validate.

For ASCII, UTF-8 and HTML, canonicalization follows the File Transfer Protocol text conventions and the 8-bit NVT-ASCII form. Lines MUST end with CRLF, trailing spaces MUST NOT appear on a line, and trailing blank lines MUST NOT appear at the end of the file. Characters outside 0x20 to 0x7E MUST NOT be changed, except by the line-ending rules, so the form-feed (0x0C) is kept. Any leading Byte Order Mark (U+FEFF) and any operating-system end-of-file marker MUST NOT be processed by the signature algorithm.

XML files should already follow the W3C guidance of using LF for line endings, so no canonicalization is needed. A robust signer MAY convert any CRLF, or CR not followed by LF, to a single LF. PDF, PostScript and EPUB are treated as a plain sequence of octets.
sections.eli5: Before stamping, everyone tidies the page the same way, with the same line breaks and no stray spaces, so two people checking get the same answer.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
IANA has registered object identifiers for three content types in the "SMI Security for S/MIME CMS Content Type (1.2.840.113549.1.9.16.1)" registry: id-ct-utf8TextWithCRLF, id-ct-htmlWithCRLF and id-ct-epub.

The security considerations and the deployment and operational considerations of RFC 5485 are both stated to be unchanged.
sections.eli5: Three new kinds of paper were added to the official list, and everything else about keeping the stamps safe stays the same.
